I have been farming these 5 mu in Quzhou for 35 years, and I know every inch of this land. My wheat is already in the ground from last autumn—it is an improved variety that my neighbor and I have been saving seed from, reliable and suited to our soil. With just two of us in the household, I cannot afford to take risks or waste labor on fancy new methods. I have a well, so when the rains fail I can pump water, but diesel for the pump costs money, so I only irrigate at the critical times when the crops will truly suffer without it.

For the wheat that is now greening up, I will topdress nitrogen at the jointing stage and again if the heads look hungry. I will irrigate three times: once when it starts growing vigorously in spring, once at heading, and once during grain filling if the weather turns dry. I will spray twice for weeds and diseases—once in early spring for grassy weeds, and once later if I see rust or aphids. I ploughed and rotavated the land before sowing last autumn, so the seedbed was good.

After we harvest the wheat in early June, there is no time to waste. I will rotavate the stubble quickly and plant hybrid maize seed the same day or the next—the summer heat here does not wait. For the maize, I will put down compound fertilizer at planting and then topdress with urea at the big trumpet stage. I will irrigate twice: once to help establishment if June is dry, and once at tasseling when the ears are setting—that is the make-or-break moment. One spray for weeds and insects should be enough if I watch the fields closely. I expect my wheat to yield around 500 jin per mu, and the maize about 550 jin per mu in a normal year. These are modest but honest expectations from this soil.
